background.speaker: SPEAKER_03
background.text: When we talk about women and the rise in the military general, what is the one thing that really needs to get through, that the general public needs to understand about how difficult it is and how tough it is to make this climb?

background.speaker: [target]
background.text: You know, my book is more about leadership than gender. And I say this to all men and women, and anyone in any profession. You know, if you get dissuaded from something you really believe in, something you think you can do, something you're very passionate about, they win. If people derail you from something you wanna do, they win. So my message is, if you really believe it, if you really wanna do something, then you drive on, because you can do it.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_02
background.text: Then how do you instill that leadership in people though? Because we are told every single day that we talk here, when we talk about the political system these days especially, we keep hearing that there's a lack of leadership. So then knowing full well that that's what the military needs to train, how do you get that type of training not only through to people trying to rise in the military, but trying to rise in politics as well in business? It's where we desperately need leadership.

ground_truth: I think it all starts, for me, at least in my family. You know, mom and dad, values-based family. Dad was a decorated veteran himself, who I respected, admired, and looked up to. My mother, a religious person, raised six kids on her own, while dad was out fighting three conflicts - the second world war, the conflict in East Asia, and the Southeast Asian conflict. And so coming from a values-based family with kids, what I realized is when I joined the military, which was something I never anticipated doing, that I was really joining a values-based organization, one where you take an oath, one where you are subject to the military justice code, which governs your behavior both in uniform and out of uniform, and one which is full of standards. How you wear your hair, how you wear your uniform, how you dress, how many push-ups you can do, how fast can you run. So an organization that's values-based, standards-based. And what I found coming in through the military is I expected, as a woman, to have to exceed those standards to prove myself. To get credibility. But the reality is that all the good leaders that I served with exceeded those standards. They lived by higher standards.
